claim: Sexual reproduction partners are rarely the same.
source: The two partners required for sexual reproduction are rarely the same.
evidence: This is a general statement presented in the abstract without specific data or citations in this sentence.

claim: Species lacking sexual dimorphism possess self-incompatible gametes determined at mating-type regions of suppressed recombination.
source: This pattern extends to species which lack sexual dimorphism yet possess self-incompatible gametes determined at mating-type regions of suppressed recombination, likely precursors of sex chromosomes.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge in the field, drawing on the broader literature context.

claim: Mating-type regions of suppressed recombination are likely precursors of sex chromosomes.
source: This pattern extends to species which lack sexual dimorphism yet possess self-incompatible gametes determined at mating-type regions of suppressed recombination, likely precursors of sex chromosomes.
evidence: This is presented as an inference based on evolutionary understanding.

claim: The model identifies factors that determine the capacity of cells to send and receive signals.
source: We develop a model of ligand-receptor dynamics, and identify factors that determine the capacity of cells to send and receive signals.
evidence: This describes the methodology and findings of the current study.

claim: The model specifies conditions favoring the evolution of gametes producing ligand and receptor asymmetrically.
source: The model specifies conditions favoring the evolution of gametes producing ligand and receptor asymmetrically and shows how these are affected by recombination.
evidence: This describes findings from the model presented in the study.

claim: Conditions favoring asymmetric signaling also favor tight linkage of ligand and receptor loci in distinct linkage groups when recombination rate evolves.
source: When the recombination rate evolves, the conditions favoring asymmetric signaling also favor tight linkage of ligand and receptor loci in distinct linkage groups.
evidence: This is a finding from the evolutionary model presented in the study.

claim: Selection for asymmetric gamete signaling could be the first step in the evolution of non-recombinant mating-type loci.
source: These results suggest that selection for asymmetric gamete signaling could be the first step in the evolution of non-recombinant mating-type loci, paving the road for the evolution of anisogamy and sexes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model results presented in the study.

claim: The sexual process is asymmetric with partnering cells exhibiting genetic, physiological or behavioral differences, with few exceptions.
source: With few exceptions, the sexual process is asymmetric with partnering cells exhibiting genetic, physiological or behavioral differences.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The origins of sexual asymmetry in eukaryotes trace back to unicellular organisms with isogametes lacking any size or mobility difference in the fusing cells.
source: The origins of sexual asymmetry in eukaryotes trace back to unicellular organisms with isogametes lacking any size or mobility difference in the fusing cells (Parker et al., 1972; Bell, 1978; Charlesworth, 1978; Hoekstra, 1987; Randerson and Hurst, 2001; Lehtonen et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Isogamous organisms are divided into genetically distinct mating types determined by several mating type specific genes that reside in regions of suppressed recombination.
source: Isogamous organisms are divided into genetically distinct mating types, determined by several mating type specific genes that reside in regions of suppressed recombination (Fraser et al., 2004; Ahmed et al., 2014; Branco et al., 2017; Branco et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Morphologically identical gametes mate disassortatively, scarcely ever with members of the same mating type.
source: The morphologically identical gametes mate disassortatively, scarcely ever with members of the same mating type.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about isogamous mating systems.

claim: Only individuals of a different mating type are eligible mating partners in isogamous organisms.
source: It follows that only individuals of a different mating type are eligible mating partners.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of disassortative mating.

claim: Mating type systems restrict the pool of potential partners to those of a different mating type, introducing a major cost.
source: This arrangement poses a paradox as it restricts the pool of potential partners to those of a different mating type, introducing a major cost (Hoekstra, 1987).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and represents a recognized paradox in the field.

claim: Mating types could serve as a restrictive mechanism preventing matings between related individuals thereby avoiding the deleterious consequences of inbreeding.
source: Mating types could serve as a restrictive mechanism preventing matings between related individuals thereby avoiding the deleterious consequences of inbreeding (Charlesworth and Charlesworth, 1979; Uyenoyama, 1988; Czárán and Hoekstra, 2004).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mating types facilitate uniparental inheritance of mitochondria, which leads to improved contribution of the mitochondrial genome to cell fitness.
source: Another idea is that mating types facilitate uniparental inheritance of mitochondria, which leads to improved contribution of the mitochondrial genome to cell fitness (Hastings, 1992; Hurst and Hamilton, 1992; Hutson and Law, 1993; Hurst, 1996; Hadjivasiliou et al., 2012; Hadjivasiliou et al., 2013; Christie et al., 2015; Christie and Beekman, 2017a).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Several species maintain mating types despite inbreeding being the rule.
source: Nevertheless, the existence of several species where inbreeding (Billiard et al., 2011; Perrin, 2012) or biparental inheritance of mitochondria (Billiard et al., 2011; Wilson and Xu, 2012) are the rule but nonetheless maintain mating types, indicates that these ideas may not alone explain the evolution of mating types.
evidence: This observation is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Several species maintain mating types despite biparental inheritance of mitochondria being the rule.
source: Nevertheless, the existence of several species where inbreeding (Billiard et al., 2011; Perrin, 2012) or biparental inheritance of mitochondria (Billiard et al., 2011; Wilson and Xu, 2012) are the rule but nonetheless maintain mating types, indicates that these ideas may not alone explain the evolution of mating types.
evidence: This observation is supported by citations.

claim: Inbreeding avoidance and mitochondrial inheritance hypotheses may not alone explain the evolution of mating types.
source: Nevertheless, the existence of several species where inbreeding (Billiard et al., 2011; Perrin, 2012) or biparental inheritance of mitochondria (Billiard et al., 2011; Wilson and Xu, 2012) are the rule but nonetheless maintain mating types, indicates that these ideas may not alone explain the evolution of mating types.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited observations.

claim: Mating types are determined by the molecular system regulating gamete interactions.
source: An alternative hypothesis is that mating types are determined by the molecular system regulating gamete interactions (Hoekstra, 1987; Hadjivasiliou et al., 2015; Hadjivasiliou and Pomiankowski, 2016).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by citations.

claim: Gamete interactions have been shown to be more efficient when operating in an asymmetric manner.
source: Such interactions dictate the success of mating by guiding partner attraction and recognition and the process of cell fusion, and have been shown to be more efficient when operating in an asymmetric manner (Hadjivasiliou et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Diffusible molecules are often employed as signals that guide synchronous entry to gametogenesis or as chemoattractants.
source: For example, diffusible molecules are often employed as signals that guide synchronous entry to gametogenesis or as chemoattractants (Tsubo, 1961; Maier, 1993; Kuhlmann et al., 1997; Merlini et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Secreting and sensing the same diffusible molecule impedes the ability of cells to accurately detect external signals and makes partner finding many-fold slower.
source: Secreting and sensing the same diffusible molecule impedes the ability of cells to accurately detect external signals and makes partner finding many-fold slower (Hadjivasiliou et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Secreting and detecting the same molecule in cell colonies can prevent individuals responding to signals from others.
source: In addition, secreting and detecting the same molecule in cell colonies can prevent individuals responding to signals from others (Youk and Lim, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Sexual signaling and communication in isogamous species are universally asymmetric.
source: Our previous review revealed that sexual signaling and communication in isogamous species are universally asymmetric (Hadjivasiliou and Pomiankowski, 2016).
evidence: This statement refers to findings from a prior review by the authors.

claim: Asymmetric signaling applies throughout the sexual process from signals that lead to gametic differentiation, to attraction via diffusible pheromones and interactions via surface bound molecules during cell fusion.
source: This applies throughout the sexual process from signals that lead to gametic differentiation, to attraction via diffusible pheromones and interactions via surface bound molecules during cell fusion (Hadjivasiliou and Pomiankowski, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The employment of membrane bound ligands during sexual signaling is universal.
source: The employment of membrane bound ligands during sexual signaling is universal, whereas diffusible signals are not (Hadjivasiliou and Pomiankowski, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Diffusible signals during sexual signaling are not universal.
source: The employment of membrane bound ligands during sexual signaling is universal, whereas diffusible signals are not (Hadjivasiliou and Pomiankowski, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Ligands only undergo localized diffusion in several yeast and other unicellular eukaryotes.
source: Receptors remain bound to the cell surface and ligands only undergo localized diffusion (Figure 1) as is the case in several yeast and other unicellular eukaryotes (Cappellaro et al., 1991; Wilson et al., 1999; Phadke and Zufall, 2009; Merlini et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and refers to Figure 1.

claim: When interacting cells produce ligand and receptor symmetrically, the ligand will bind to receptors on its own membrane as well as those on the other cell, which may impair intercellular signaling.
source: (a) When the interacting cells produce ligand and receptor symmetrically, the ligand will bind to receptors on its own membrane as well as those on the other cell. This may impair intercellular signaling.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1a and explained in the caption.

claim: Producing the ligand and receptor in an asymmetric manner resolves the issue of self-binding impairing intercellular signaling.
source: (b) Producing the ligand and receptor in an asymmetric manner resolves this issue.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1b and explained in the caption.

claim: For low degradation rates, the removal of available molecules is dominated by self-binding.
source: For low degradation rates (γ small), the removal of available molecules is dominated by self-binding (k+) (Equations (1) and (2) and Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical model and shown in Figure 2.

claim: A lower degradation rate leads to higher levels of ligand and receptor.
source: At the same time, a lower degradation rate leads to higher levels of ligand and receptor (Figure 2a) even if the relative drop of free ligand and receptor is steeper as k+ increases (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The fold-increase in W12 is large even when self-binding confers no cost (n=0).
source: The fold-increase in W12 is large even when self-binding confers no cost (n=0), while larger values for n ramp up the costs (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2c.

claim: If cells produce the ligand and receptor asymmetrically, self-binding ceases to be a problem in receiving incoming signals.
source: If cells produce the ligand and receptor asymmetrically, self-binding ceases to be a problem in receiving incoming signals.
evidence: This is an inference from the model results.

claim: A resident cell with production rates (νL,νR,νl,νr)res=(1,1,0,0) cannot be invaded by any single mutant.
source: It follows that (νL,νR,νl,νr)=(1,1,0,0) cannot be invaded by any single mutant.
evidence: This is derived from the analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Starting from a population where all cells are symmetric producers of only one ligand and receptor, the population evolves to one of two equilibria.
source: Starting from a population where all cells are symmetric producers of only one ligand and receptor, (νL,νR,νl,νr)=(1,1,0,0), the population evolves to one of two equilibria (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4a from the evolutionary simulations.

claim: E1 equilibrium is characterized by s*≈1 where all cells produce the ligand and receptor symmetrically.
source: E1 where s*≈1 and all cells produce the ligand and receptor symmetrically (νL,νR,νl,νr)≈(1,1,0,0)
evidence: This describes one of the equilibria found in the simulations.

claim: E2 equilibrium is characterized by s*≈0 where the population is divided into ligand and receptor producing cells.
source: E2 where s*≈0 and the population is divided into ligand and receptor producing cells, with equal frequencies of (νL,νR,νl,νr)≈(1,0,0,1) and (νL,νR,νl,νr)≈(0,1,1,0) (Figure 4b,c).
evidence: This describes the second equilibrium found in the simulations, shown in Figures 4b and 4c.

claim: Equilibria with intermediate values of s* are not found.
source: Equilibria with intermediate values of s* are not found.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results.

claim: E1 persists and no asymmetry evolves when k+ (the intracellular ligand-receptor binding coefficient) is small.
source: E1 persists and no asymmetry evolves when k+ (the intracellular ligand-receptor binding coefficient) is small (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4d.

claim: When k+ is small, the concentration of self-bound ligand-receptor complex is small and there is little cost of self-signaling.
source: In this case, the concentration of self-bound ligand-receptor complex is small (Equation (6)) and there is little cost of self-signaling (Equation (8)), so there is weak selection in favor of asymmetry.
evidence: This is an inference from the mathematical model.

claim: When the population is at E1, asymmetric mutants are slightly deleterious on their own.
source: When the population is at E1, asymmetric mutants are slightly deleterious on their own (Figure 3a).
evidence: This refers to results shown in Figure 3a.

claim: For larger values of k+, self-binding dominates and restricts between cell signaling, promoting the evolution of asymmetry.
source: The opposite is true for larger values of k+, as self-binding now dominates and restricts between cell signaling, promoting the evolution of asymmetry (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The transition from E1 to E2 occurs at a smaller value of k+ when the degradation rate (γ) is decreased.
source: The transition from E1 to E2 occurs at a smaller value of k+ when the degradation rate (γ) is decreased (Figure 4d), as the effective removal of free ligand and receptor depends more strongly on intercellular binding (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4d and explained by reference to Figure 2.

claim: The mutation rate affects the value of k+ at which the transition from E1 to E2 occurs.
source: Furthermore, the mutation rate affects the value of k+ at which the transition from E1 to E2 occurs.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulations.

claim: The transition from E1 to E2 when mutation rates are smaller occurs at larger k+.
source: The transition from E1 to E2 when mutation rates are smaller occurs at larger k+ (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The threshold value of the within cell binding rate beyond which symmetric signaling evolves to asymmetric signaling increases when kb becomes much larger than k+/k-.
source: For example, the threshold value of the within cell binding rate beyond which symmetric signaling (E1) evolves to asymmetric signaling (E2, Figure 4a) increases when kb becomes much larger than k+/k- (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The threshold value for evolution of asymmetric signaling is smaller for larger values of n.
source: Furthermore, this threshold value is smaller for larger values of n indicating that asymmetric signaling is more likely to evolve when the cost for self-signaling is higher (larger n, Figure 4e).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Asymmetric signaling can evolve even when self-binding carries no cost (n=0).
source: However, asymmetric signaling can evolve even when self-binding carries no cost (n=0) as high rates of self-binding can restrict the number of ligand and receptor molecules free for between cell interactions (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4e.

claim: When the two ligands (or receptors) exhibit synergy, a signaling asymmetry evolves more easily.
source: When the two ligands (or receptors) exhibit synergy so that νL+νl<α and νR+νr<α for α>1, a signaling asymmetry evolves more easily (for smaller values of k+, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: When the two ligands (or receptors) compete with one another, the reverse dynamics are observed.
source: The reverse dynamics are observed when the two ligands (or receptors) compete with one another (νL+νl<α and νR+νr<α for α<1 ) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both E1 and E2 are evolutionary stable states.
source: The observations above suggest that both E1 and E2 are evolutionary stable states and the transition from E1 to E2 depends on the mutational process, drift and the parameters that determine signaling interactions.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: The basin of attraction for E2 is larger when k+ and p are high and γ is small.
source: The basin of attraction for E2 (and so asymmetric signaling roles) is larger when k+ and p are high and γ is small (Figure 5a–d), as predicted analytically (Figures 2 and 3) and in accordance with our findings when mutations were continuous (Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 and consistent with earlier analytical and simulation results.

claim: When mutants are introduced at a lower frequency, the probability that they meet one another before they are lost by drift increases.
source: When mutants are introduced at a lower frequency (compare Figure 5a–b), the probability that they meet one another before they are lost by drift increases.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing Figure 5a and 5b.

claim: An asymmetry in both ligand and receptor production is necessary for the evolution of a signaling asymmetry.
source: It follows that an asymmetry in both ligand and receptor production is necessary for the evolution of a signaling asymmetry as predicted analytically (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is an inference from the adaptive dynamics results, consistent with Figure 3a.

claim: When the population evolves to E2, s* becomes larger as the recombination rate (ρ) increases.
source: When the population evolves to E2, s* becomes larger as the recombination rate, (ρ), increases (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7b.

claim: For low recombination rates (ρ≤0.1), the population largely consists of equal frequencies of (1,0,0,1) and (0,1,1,0) cells.
source: For low recombination rates (ρ≤0.1), the population largely consists of equal frequencies of (1,0,0,1) and (0,1,1,0) cells, producing the ligand and receptor asymmetrically.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulations with recombination.

claim: A small percentage of recombinant cells produce conspecific pairs of ligand and receptor at low recombination rates.
source: A small percentage of recombinant cells produce conspecific pairs of ligand and receptor (νL,νR,νl,νr)=(1,1,0,0) and (0,0,1,1) (Figure 7b,c).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 7b and 7c.

claim: Higher recombination rates (ρ≥0.3) push s*=0.5 at E2.
source: Higher recombination rates (ρ≥0.3) push s*=0.5 at E2 (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7b.

claim: At high recombination rates, there is a predominance of (νL,νR,νl,νr)=(1,0.5,0,0.5) and (0,0.5,1,0.5) cells at equal frequencies.
source: Ηere, there is a predominance of (νL,νR,νl,νr)=(1,0.5,0,0.5) and (0,0.5,1,0.5) cells at equal frequencies (or (0.5,1,0.5,0) and (0.5,0,0.5,1) by symmetry).
evidence: This is an observation from the simulations with high recombination.

claim: The arrangement at high recombination rates maintains some degree of asymmetry even with free recombination (ρ=0.5).
source: Note that this arrangement maintains some degree of asymmetry even with free recombination (ρ=0.5).
evidence: This is an observation from the simulations.

claim: The recombination rate evolves to ρ*=0 whenever E2 was reached from E1 in the no recombination analysis.
source: The recombination rate evolves to ρ*=0 whenever E2 was reached from E1 in the no recombination analysis.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulations where recombination rate evolves.

claim: Tight linkage between receptor and ligand genes is favored under conditions where E2 evolves.
source: Under these conditions, tight linkage between receptor and ligand genes is favored (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8a.

claim: Asymmetric signaling roles coevolve together with the recombination rate.
source: Furthermore, asymmetric signaling roles coevolve together with the recombination rate.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulations where both traits evolve.

claim: When k+ is large (k+=10), signal asymmetry rapidly evolves and this is followed by a sharp drop in the recombination rate.
source: For example, when k+ is large (k+=10), signal asymmetry rapidly evolves; s moves away from one and this is followed by a sharp drop in the recombination rate (Figure 8b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8b.

claim: When selection for asymmetric signaling is weaker (k+=3), it takes longer for the asymmetric types to co-evolve.
source: These dynamics are similar when k+ is smaller (k+=3, Figure 8c) and selection for asymmetry is weaker. However, it now takes longer for the asymmetric types to co-evolve (Figure 8c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8c.

claim: When selection for asymmetric signaling is even weaker (k+=1), no asymmetry evolves and the recombination rate fluctuates randomly.
source: When selection for asymmetric signaling is even weaker (k+=1, Figure 8d), no asymmetry evolves (s remains at 1) and the recombination rate fluctuates randomly between its minimum and maximum value as one would expect in the case of a neutral allele.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8d.

claim: An asymmetry in ligand and receptor production evolves as a response to selection for swift gamete communication and mating.
source: In this work we show that an asymmetry in ligand and receptor production evolves as a response to selection for swift gamete communication and mating.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: The same conditions favoring asymmetric signaling select for tight linkage between the receptor and ligand genes.
source: Furthermore, the same conditions favoring asymmetric signaling select for tight linkage between the receptor and ligand genes.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: Selection for asymmetric signaling roles could have played an important role in the early evolution of gamete differentiation and identity.
source: Our findings indicate that selection for asymmetric signaling roles could have played an important role in the early evolution of gamete differentiation and identity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Gene duplication followed by mutation is a well established route to novelty evolution.
source: Gene duplication followed by mutation is a well established route to novelty evolution (Susumu, 1970; Zhang, 2003; Magadum et al., 2013) and could explain the co-existence of two pairs of ligand and receptor in our system.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Individual cells could produce multiple ligands and receptors which evolve independently, as is the case in some basidiomycete fungi.
source: Alternatively, individual cells could produce multiple ligands and receptors which evolve independently, as is the case in some basidiomycete fungi (Fowler and Vaillancourt, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The co-existence of mating types with pansexuals is rare in natural populations.
source: This could explain why the co-existence of mating types with pansexuals is rare in natural populations (Billiard et al., 2011; Billiard et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations and is an inference from the model results.

claim: In previous models, pansexual types were very hard to eliminate due to negative frequency dependent selection.
source: This is in contrast to previous models where pansexual types were very hard to eliminate due to negative frequency dependent selection (Hoekstra, 1982; Czárán and Hoekstra, 2004; Hadjivasiliou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the mitochondrial inheritance model, uniparental inheritance raises fitness not only in individuals that carry genes for uniparental inheritance but also for pansexual individuals.
source: For example, in the case of the mitochondrial inheritance model, uniparental inheritance raises fitness not only in individuals that carry genes for uniparental inheritance but also for pansexual individuals (benefits 'leak' to biparental individuals) (Hadjivasiliou et al., 2013; Christie and Beekman, 2017b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The spread of self-incompatibility reduces the population mutation load, and so reduces the need for inbreeding avoidance.
source: A similar pattern is seen with inbreeding avoidance because the spread of self-incompatibility reduces the population mutation load, and so reduces the need for inbreeding avoidance (Czárán and Hoekstra, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: In the present model there is positive frequency dependent selection where the spread of asymmetric signalers generates stronger selection for further asymmetry.
source: These dynamics are reversed in the present model where there is positive frequency dependent selection. The spread of asymmetric signalers generates stronger selection for further asymmetry (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: This is an observation from the model results shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Even though recombination between the two asymmetric types generates symmetric recombinant offspring, these are disfavored and eliminated by selection.
source: This also occurs when there is recombination (Figures 7 and 8). Even though recombination between the two asymmetric types generates symmetric recombinant offspring, these are disfavored and eliminated by selection.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulations with recombination shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: The mitochondrial inheritance and inbreeding avoidance models are unlikely to generate strong selection for suppressed recombination.
source: These observations suggest that the mitochondrial inheritance and inbreeding avoidance models are unlikely to generate strong selection for suppressed recombination which is the hallmark of mating types.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing the present model with previous models.

claim: Mating type identity in unicellular eukaryotes is determined by mating type loci that typically carry a number of genes.
source: Mating type identity in unicellular eukaryotes is determined by mating type loci that typically carry a number of genes (Billiard et al., 2012; Hadjivasiliou and Pomiankowski, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Suppressed recombination at the mating type locus is a common feature across the evolutionary tree.
source: Suppressed recombination at the mating type locus is a common feature across the evolutionary tree (Branco et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The work predicts the co-evolution of mating type specific signaling roles and suppressed recombination.
source: Our work predicts the co-evolution of mating type specific signaling roles and suppressed recombination with selection favoring linkage between loci responsible for signaling and an asymmetry in signaling roles.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's predictions.

claim: Selection for asymmetric signaling could be the very first step in the evolution of tight linkage between genes that control mating type identity.
source: This finding suggests that selection for asymmetric signaling could be the very first step in the evolution of tight linkage between genes that control mating type identity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: In yeasts, the only genes in the mating type locus code for the production of ligand and receptor molecules.
source: In yeasts, the only genes in the mating type locus code for the production of ligand and receptor molecules (Merlini et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Mating type loci with suppressed recombination are precursors to sex chromosomes.
source: Evidence across species suggests that mating type loci with suppressed recombination are precursors to sex chromosomes (Menkis et al., 2008; Geng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The work provides crucial insights about the origin of sex chromosomes.
source: In this way our work provides crucial insights about the origin of sex chromosomes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's implications.

claim: Opposite mating type gametes often utilize diffusible signals to attract partners.
source: For example, opposite mating type gametes often utilize diffusible signals to attract partners (Luporini et al., 1995; Tsuchikane et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The inclusion of long range signals such as those used in sexual chemotaxis will provide further benefits for asymmetric signaling roles and mating types.
source: The inclusion of long range signals such as those used in sexual chemotaxis will provide further benefits for asymmetric signaling roles and mating types (Hadjivasiliou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculation about future work, supported by a citation.

claim: The number of mating types varies greatly across species and is likely to depend on the frequency of sexual reproduction and mutation rates.
source: Furthermore the number of mating types varies greatly across species and is likely to depend on the frequency of sexual reproduction and mutation rates (Constable and Kokko, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The evolution of asymmetric gamete signaling and mating types is contingent upon the mutation rate.
source: Our analysis revealed that the evolution of asymmetric gamete signaling and mating types is contingent upon the mutation rate.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis.

claim: When the population size is small and mutation rates are low, there is a low probability that individuals carrying asymmetric mutations in opposite directions are segregating at the same time.
source: When the population size is small and mutation rates are low, there is a low probability that individuals carrying asymmetric mutations in opposite directions are segregating at the same time.
evidence: This is an inference from the model dynamics.

claim: Increasing the population size or the mutation rate would enhance the probability of co-segregation, making the evolution of asymmetric signaling more likely.
source: Increasing the population size or the mutation rate would enhance the probability of co-segregation, making the evolution of asymmetric signaling more likely.
evidence: This is an inference from the model dynamics.

claim: In an infinite population the evolution of signaling asymmetry should be independent of the mutation rate.
source: In an infinite population the evolution of signaling asymmetry should be independent of the mutation rate.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction.

claim: Unicellular eukaryotes undergo several rounds of asexual growth (tens to thousands) between each sexual reproduction.
source: Finally, it is worth noting that unicellular eukaryotes undergo several rounds of asexual growth (tens to thousands) between each sexual reproduction (Hadjivasiliou et al., 2016b; Constable and Kokko, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The effective mutation rate between sexual rounds will end up being orders of magnitude higher than the mutation rates at each vegetative step.
source: It follows that the effective mutation rate between sexual rounds will end up being orders of magnitude higher than the mutation rates at each vegetative step.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation about asexual growth cycles.

claim: Selection for swift and robust signaling interactions between mating cells can lead to the evolution of self-incompatible mating types determined at non-recombinant mating type loci.
source: Taken together our findings suggest that selection for swift and robust signaling interactions between mating cells can lead to the evolution of self-incompatible mating types determined at non-recombinant mating type loci.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study.

claim: The fundamental selection for asymmetric signaling between mating cells could be the very first step in the evolution of sexual asymmetry, paving the way for the evolution of anisogamy, sex chromosomes and sexes.
source: We conclude that the fundamental selection for asymmetric signaling between mating cells could be the very first step in the evolution of sexual asymmetry, paving the way for the evolution of anisogamy, sex chromosomes and sexes.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.
